title: Sex differences in the association of late-life blood pressure decline with postmortem brain vessel pathology
title_zh: 晚年血压下降与死后脑血管病变关联的性别差异
abstract: Although hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for cerebrovascular disease, less is known about the relation of late-life change in blood pressure (BP) and cerebrovascular pathology beyond brain infarcts. Our previous work found sex-specific associations between declining systolic BP (SBP) and cognitive decline in late-life, suggesting that cerebrovascular pathology may be an upstream contributor to these sex differences. However, postmortem studies have not examined whether BP change differentially relates to vascular brain pathology in men and women, despite well-established sex differences in BP trajectories and cerebrovascular pathology. We examined associations between change in late-life BP and postmortem cerebrovascular (arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis, and cerebral amyloid angiopathy) pathology from 2033 community-dwelling older adults (mean baseline age = 79.7 [SD = 7.1] years; 69% women) from four longitudinal cohort studies with brain autopsy (mean age-at-death = 89.8 [6.6] years). Person-specific late-life BP slopes estimated from annual clinical evaluations over an average of 9.1 [5.7] years were entered in ordinal regressions adjusted for age-at-death, sex, antihypertensive medication use, and BP slope × sex, age-at-death × sex, and BP slope × age-at-death interactions. Faster SBP decline was associated with greater severity of arteriolosclerosis (OR = 1.24, 95%CI 1.08-1.42) and atherosclerosis (OR = 1.41, 95%CI 1.22-1.63). A sex × SBP slope interaction (p = 0.01) revealed a stronger association of SBP decline with arteriolosclerosis severity in women than men. This longitudinal, clinical-pathologic study of older decedents showed sex differences in the association of declining SBP in late-life with severity of arteriolosclerosis, extending prior associations with cognitive decline to cerebrovascular pathology, and suggests potential for longitudinal BP monitoring for precision medicine approaches in cerebrovascular disease risk stratification.
abstract_zh: 尽管高血压是脑血管疾病的首要可修饰危险因素，但关于晚年血压（BP）变化与脑血管病变（除脑梗外）的关系知之甚少。我们先前的研究发现，晚年收缩压（SBP）下降与认知下降存在性别特异性关联，提示脑血管病变可能是这些性别差异的上游贡献因素。然而，尽管男女在血压轨迹和脑血管病变方面存在已确立的差异，但尸检研究尚未检查BP变化在男女中是否与脑血管病变的不同相关性。我们研究了晚年BP变化与死后脑血管（动脉小动脉硬化、动脉粥样硬化和脑β-淀粉样血管病）病变的关联，样本来自2033名居住社区的老年人（平均基线年龄=79.7 [SD=7.1] 年；69%女性），这些人来自四个随访队列，并接受了脑组织解剖（平均死亡年龄=89.8 [6.6] 年）。从年度临床评估中估算的个体化晚年BP斜率，平均随访9.1 [5.7] 年，被纳入调整了死亡年龄、性别、降压药使用以及BP斜率×性别、死亡年龄×性别和BP斜率×死亡年龄交互作用的有序回归模型中。更快的SBP下降与动脉小动脉硬化（OR=1.24，95%CI 1.08-1.42）和动脉粥样硬化（OR=1.41，95%CI 1.22-1.63）的严重程度增加相关。SBP斜率×性别交互作用（p=0.01）揭示了SBP下降与动脉小动脉硬化严重程度之间的更强关联在女性中优于男性。这项针对老年去世者的纵向临床病理研究显示，晚年SBP下降与动脉小动脉硬化严重程度存在性别差异，将先前与认知下降的关联延伸至脑血管病变，并提示在脑血管疾病危险分层中进行精准医学方法的纵向血压监测潜力。
